## AI foundations

_The model-side vocabulary everything else sits on._

### Artificial intelligence (AI)

Umbrella term for systems that perform tasks associated with human cognition: perception, language, reasoning, planning. In current industry usage it almost always means machine-learned models, especially large neural networks.

See also: [Machine learning (ML)](#machine-learning-ml), [Large language model (LLM)](#large-language-model-llm)

### Machine learning (ML)

Building systems that learn behavior from data rather than hand-written rules. The three classic paradigms are supervised learning (labeled examples), unsupervised learning (structure in unlabeled data) and reinforcement learning (learning from reward through interaction).

See also: [Reinforcement learning (RL)](#reinforcement-learning-rl), [Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)](#supervised-fine-tuning-sft)

### Neural network

A function built from layers of weighted sums followed by nonlinear activations. Its weights are adjusted during training so the output moves closer to a target. Deep learning means networks with many layers.

See also: [Parameters / weights](#parameters--weights), [Gradient descent](#gradient-descent)

### Parameters / weights

Notation: `θ`

The learned numbers inside a model. Model size is quoted in parameters (for example 70B = 70 billion). In RL papers the policy is written π_θ to show it is controlled by the parameters θ.

See also: [Policy](#policy)

### Loss function

Notation: `L(θ)`

A scalar measuring how wrong the model is on a batch. Training minimizes it. Pretraining uses next-token cross-entropy; RL replaces a fixed target with an objective built from rewards.

See also: [Gradient descent](#gradient-descent), [Pretraining](#pretraining)

### Gradient descent

Notation: `θ ← θ − η∇L`

The optimization loop behind all of this: compute how the loss changes with each parameter (the gradient), then step the parameters a little in the opposite direction. η is the learning rate. Adam/AdamW are the standard variants.

See also: [Backpropagation](#backpropagation), [Loss function](#loss-function)

### Backpropagation

The algorithm that computes gradients efficiently by applying the chain rule backward through the network's layers.

See also: [Gradient descent](#gradient-descent)

### Transformer

The neural architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017) behind nearly every modern LLM. It processes a sequence of tokens with stacked attention and feed-forward layers, and parallelizes well on GPUs, which is what made large-scale pretraining practical.

See also: [Attention](#attention), [Token](#token)

### Attention

Also: self-attention · Notation: `softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V`

The mechanism that lets each token weigh every other token in the context when computing its representation. Cost grows with the square of sequence length, which is why long context is expensive.

See also: [Transformer](#transformer), [Context window](#context-window)

### Token

The unit a language model reads and writes: usually a word piece of about 3–4 characters of English. A tokenizer maps text to token IDs. Pricing, context limits and RL rollout budgets are all counted in tokens.

See also: [Context window](#context-window), [Rollout](#rollout)

### Embedding

A dense vector representing a token, document or other object, positioned so that similar things are close together. Embeddings power semantic search and retrieval.

See also: [Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)](#retrieval-augmented-generation-rag)

### Context window

The maximum number of tokens a model can take into account at once, covering prompt, tool outputs and its own response. Long-horizon agentic tasks (large codebases, multi-step exploits) press hard against this limit.

See also: [Horizon](#horizon), [Agent (AI)](#agent-ai)

### Logits & softmax

Notation: `p = softmax(z / T)`

Logits z are the raw scores the model assigns to every possible next token. Softmax turns them into a probability distribution. Log-probabilities of generated tokens are the quantity that RL algorithms push up or down.

See also: [Temperature](#temperature), [Policy gradient](#policy-gradient)

### Temperature

Notation: `T`

Divides logits before sampling. Low T approaches greedy, deterministic output; higher T gives more diverse samples. RL training uses nonzero temperature so rollouts differ and the algorithm has variation to learn from.

See also: [Exploration vs. exploitation](#exploration-vs-exploitation), [Logits & softmax](#logits--softmax)

### Large language model (LLM)

A transformer trained on very large text corpora to predict the next token, then usually post-trained to follow instructions. Frontier LLMs are the models RL environments are built to improve.

See also: [Pretraining](#pretraining), [Post-training](#post-training)

### Foundation model

A large model pretrained on broad data that is adapted to many downstream tasks. Often used interchangeably with base model or frontier model.

See also: [Pretraining](#pretraining)

### Pretraining

The first and most compute-heavy phase: next-token prediction over trillions of tokens. It produces a base model with broad knowledge but no reliable instruction-following or goal-directed behavior.

See also: [Post-training](#post-training), [Scaling laws](#scaling-laws)

### Inference

Running a trained model to produce outputs. In RL, generating rollouts is inference, and it often dominates training cost for LLM RL.

See also: [Rollout](#rollout), [Test-time compute](#test-time-compute)

### Scaling laws

Empirical power-law relationships between model performance and compute, data and parameter count (Kaplan et al. 2020; Chinchilla, Hoffmann et al. 2022). Labs increasingly discuss scaling RL compute and test-time compute as additional axes beyond pretraining.

See also: [Test-time compute](#test-time-compute), [Compute (FLOPs)](#compute-flops)

### Compute (FLOPs)

Floating-point operations. Training runs are sized in total FLOPs and GPU-hours. It is a lab's scarcest resource, so every environment competes for a share of the RL compute budget.

> **In the room:** When a lab asks whether an environment is worth the compute, they mean: does signal per GPU-hour beat their other options?

See also: [Scaling laws](#scaling-laws)

### Mixture of Experts (MoE)

An architecture where each token is routed to a small subset of expert sub-networks. Total parameters can be very large while compute per token stays modest.

See also: [Parameters / weights](#parameters--weights)

### Distillation

Training a smaller student model to imitate a larger teacher model's outputs or probability distributions. It is common for turning RL-trained reasoning ability into cheaper models.

See also: [Synthetic data](#synthetic-data)

### Hallucination

Fluent output that is false or unsupported, such as invented APIs, CVEs or code paths. In security tasks, hallucinated findings are the core reason graders must verify claims rather than trust them.

See also: [Grader](#grader), [False positive](#false-positive)

### Multimodal

Models that take or produce more than text, such as images, audio, video or screen pixels. Computer-use agents rely on multimodal perception.

See also: [Agent (AI)](#agent-ai)

### Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)

Fetching relevant documents at query time (often by embedding similarity) and placing them in the context so the model answers from them. It is an inference-time technique, distinct from training.

See also: [Embedding](#embedding), [Context window](#context-window)

## RL core concepts

_The formal building blocks of reinforcement learning._

### Reinforcement learning (RL)

Learning a behavior by trial and error: an agent acts in an environment, receives rewards, and adjusts its policy to maximize expected cumulative reward. No one provides the correct answer; only a score for what the agent did.

> **In the room:** For LLMs this is the shift from 'imitate good text' to 'find whatever actually works, as judged by the reward.' Environment quality becomes the bottleneck.

See also: [Agent (RL)](#agent-rl), [Environment](#environment), [Reward](#reward)

### Agent (RL)

The learner and decision-maker. In LLM RL the agent is the model being trained (the policy), sometimes wrapped in a scaffold that gives it tools.

See also: [Policy](#policy), [Scaffold / harness](#scaffold--harness)

### Environment

Everything outside the agent. It receives actions, returns new observations and emits rewards. Formally, it defines the transition dynamics and reward function of an MDP.

See also: [RL environment (for LLMs)](#rl-environment-for-llms), [Markov decision process (MDP)](#markov-decision-process-mdp)

### State / observation

Notation: `s, o`

The state s is the complete situation; an observation o is what the agent actually sees. LLM agents almost never see full state. They see a prompt plus tool outputs, which makes most real tasks partially observable.

See also: [POMDP](#pomdp)

### Action / action space

Notation: `a ∈ 𝒜`

What the agent can do. For an LLM, each token is technically an action. In agentic settings, actions are usually thought of at the level of tool calls such as running a command, editing a file or submitting an answer.

See also: [Tool use / function calling](#tool-use--function-calling)

### Reward

Notation: `r`

A scalar signal the environment emits to score behavior. The reward is the only definition of 'good' the agent gets, so everything it learns is shaped by what the reward does and does not check.

See also: [Reward hacking](#reward-hacking), [Sparse vs. dense reward](#sparse-vs-dense-reward), [Grader](#grader)

### Return

Notation: `G = Σ γᵗ rₜ`

The cumulative, usually discounted, reward from a point in time to the end of the episode. RL maximizes expected return, not the immediate reward.

See also: [Discount factor](#discount-factor)

### Discount factor

Notation: `γ ∈ [0,1]`

Down-weights future rewards. γ near 1 means far-future outcomes matter almost as much as immediate ones. LLM RL on single-answer tasks often effectively uses γ = 1.

See also: [Return](#return)

### Episode / trajectory

Notation: `τ = (s₀,a₀,r₀,s₁,…)`

One complete run from start to termination. The trajectory is the full sequence of observations, actions and rewards. In LLM work a trajectory is the full transcript: prompt, reasoning, tool calls and final answer.

See also: [Rollout](#rollout)

### Rollout

Running the current policy in the environment to generate a trajectory, or the trajectory itself. Labs talk about rollouts per task, rollout throughput and rollout cost.

> **In the room:** Environment latency directly throttles rollout throughput. Slow environments leave GPUs idle.

See also: [Episode / trajectory](#episode--trajectory), [Rollout infrastructure](#rollout-infrastructure)

### Policy

Notation: `π_θ(a | s)`

The agent's strategy: a probability distribution over actions given the state. For an LLM, the model itself is the policy, a distribution over next tokens given the context.

See also: [Parameters / weights](#parameters--weights), [Policy gradient](#policy-gradient)

### Value function

Notation: `V^π(s)`

The expected return from state s if the agent follows policy π afterward. It measures how good a situation is.

See also: [Q-function](#q-function), [Actor-critic](#actor-critic)

### Q-function

Also: action-value function · Notation: `Q^π(s,a)`

The expected return from taking action a in state s and then following π. It measures how good an action is in context.

See also: [Q-learning / DQN](#q-learning--dqn), [Advantage](#advantage)

### Advantage

Notation: `A(s,a) = Q(s,a) − V(s)`

How much better an action was than the policy's average in that state. Policy-gradient methods use advantage rather than raw reward, which cuts variance. GRPO estimates it by comparing a sample with its siblings.

See also: [GRPO](#grpo), [PPO](#ppo), [Baseline](#baseline)

### Baseline

Notation: `b(s)`

A value subtracted from the return in policy-gradient updates to reduce variance without introducing bias. A learned value function (critic) or a group-mean reward are common choices.

See also: [Advantage](#advantage), [GRPO](#grpo)

### Markov decision process (MDP)

Notation: `(𝒮, 𝒜, P, R, γ)`

The formal model of an RL problem: states, actions, transition probabilities P, reward function R and discount γ. 'Markov' means the next state depends only on the current state and action, not on history.

See also: [POMDP](#pomdp), [Bellman equation](#bellman-equation)

### POMDP

Also: partially observable MDP

An MDP where the agent receives observations rather than the full state. Debugging an unfamiliar binary or codebase is a POMDP: the agent must explore to learn what is true.

See also: [State / observation](#state--observation)

### Bellman equation

Notation: `V(s) = E[r + γV(s′)]`

The recursive relationship at the heart of value-based RL: a state's value equals the immediate reward plus the discounted value of the next state. Temporal-difference learning and Q-learning are built on it.

See also: [Temporal-difference (TD) learning](#temporal-difference-td-learning)

### Exploration vs. exploitation

The core tension of RL: try new actions to discover better strategies, or use what already works. If the policy never produces a success, it has nothing to reinforce.

> **In the room:** This is why task difficulty matters. Tasks the model never solves produce zero learning signal.

See also: [Pass rate / difficulty band](#pass-rate--difficulty-band), [Temperature](#temperature)

### On-policy vs. off-policy

On-policy methods (PPO, GRPO) learn only from data generated by the current policy. Off-policy methods (Q-learning) can reuse data from older policies or other sources. On-policy is standard in LLM RL, which is why fresh rollouts are needed every step.

See also: [PPO](#ppo), [Offline RL](#offline-rl)

### Model-based vs. model-free

Model-based RL learns or uses a model of the environment's dynamics to plan (AlphaZero, MuZero). Model-free RL learns a policy or value directly from experience. LLM post-training is almost entirely model-free.

See also: [Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)](#monte-carlo-tree-search-mcts)

### Credit assignment

Working out which of many earlier actions caused a later reward. It is hard when a 200-step agent trajectory gets a single pass/fail at the end.

See also: [Process reward model (PRM)](#process-reward-model-prm), [Sparse vs. dense reward](#sparse-vs-dense-reward)

### Sparse vs. dense reward

Sparse: reward only at the end, often binary (the exploit worked or it didn't). Dense: frequent partial rewards along the way. Sparse rewards are harder to hack but harder to learn from; dense rewards speed learning but add more ways to game them.

See also: [Reward shaping](#reward-shaping), [Tiered / partial-credit reward](#tiered--partial-credit-reward)

### Horizon

How many steps an episode lasts. Long-horizon tasks, such as multi-hour agentic coding or exploitation, are a frontier focus because they need planning, memory and recovery from errors.

See also: [Context window](#context-window), [Credit assignment](#credit-assignment)

### Sample efficiency

How much learning a method extracts per rollout. With expensive environments and expensive inference, sample efficiency translates directly into dollars.

See also: [Rollout](#rollout)

## RL algorithms

_Named methods you will hear in research conversations._

### Temporal-difference (TD) learning

Notation: `δ = r + γV(s′) − V(s)`

Updates value estimates toward a bootstrapped target (immediate reward plus the estimated value of the next state) instead of waiting for the episode to end. The TD error δ drives the update.

See also: [Bellman equation](#bellman-equation), [Q-learning / DQN](#q-learning--dqn)

### Q-learning / DQN

Off-policy value learning: iteratively update Q(s,a) toward r + γ·maxₐ′Q(s′,a′). DQN (DeepMind, 2013/2015) used a neural network for Q and learned Atari games from pixels. It was a landmark, but it is rarely used for LLMs.

See also: [Q-function](#q-function), [On-policy vs. off-policy](#on-policy-vs-off-policy)

### Policy gradient

Notation: `∇J = E[∇log π_θ(a|s) · A]`

Directly adjusts policy parameters to make high-advantage actions more likely. It is the family behind nearly all LLM RL: raise the log-probability of tokens in good trajectories and lower it in bad ones.

See also: [REINFORCE](#reinforce), [PPO](#ppo), [GRPO](#grpo)

### REINFORCE

The simplest policy-gradient algorithm (Williams, 1992): scale the log-probability gradient of sampled actions by the return. It is unbiased but high-variance. Variants with baselines (RLOO, ReMax) have come back for LLM training because of their simplicity.

See also: [Policy gradient](#policy-gradient), [Baseline](#baseline)

### Actor-critic

Pairs a policy (actor) with a learned value function (critic). The critic's estimate becomes the baseline for the actor's advantage. PPO as used in RLHF is an actor-critic method.

See also: [PPO](#ppo), [Value function](#value-function)

### PPO

Also: Proximal Policy Optimization · Notation: `clip(ρ, 1−ε, 1+ε)·A`

Schulman et al., 2017. A policy-gradient method that clips the probability ratio ρ between new and old policy so each update stays small and stable. It was the workhorse of original RLHF (InstructGPT) and needs a separate critic model.

See also: [GRPO](#grpo), [Actor-critic](#actor-critic), [KL penalty / reference model](#kl-penalty--reference-model)

### GRPO

Also: Group Relative Policy Optimization

Introduced with DeepSeekMath (2024) and central to DeepSeek-R1. For each prompt, sample a group of responses, score them all, and use each response's reward relative to the group mean (normalized by std) as its advantage. It drops the critic, saving memory and compute.

> **In the room:** GRPO and its descendants explain why labs want tasks with graded variation. If all samples in a group score the same (all pass or all fail), the advantage is zero and that prompt teaches nothing.

See also: [Advantage](#advantage), [PPO](#ppo), [Pass rate / difficulty band](#pass-rate--difficulty-band)

### DPO

Also: Direct Preference Optimization

Rafailov et al., 2023. Trains directly on preference pairs (chosen vs. rejected) with a classification-style loss, with no reward model and no RL loop. It is cheap and popular for style and alignment tuning, but offline, so it doesn't explore.

See also: [RLHF](#rlhf), [Preference data](#preference-data)

### Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)

A planning algorithm that builds a search tree by simulating many possible futures and backing up their results. It was core to AlphaGo and AlphaZero and is explored for LLM reasoning and theorem proving.

See also: [Model-based vs. model-free](#model-based-vs-model-free), [Self-play](#self-play)

### Imitation learning / behavior cloning

Learning a policy by copying expert demonstrations instead of optimizing reward. SFT on expert transcripts is behavior cloning. It can't exceed the demonstrator and struggles when the agent drifts into unfamiliar states.

See also: [Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)](#supervised-fine-tuning-sft)

### Inverse RL

Inferring the reward function that explains an expert's behavior. It is conceptually related to reward modeling from human preferences.

See also: [Reward model (RM)](#reward-model-rm)

### Offline RL

Learning a policy from a fixed dataset of past trajectories with no new environment interaction. It is useful when interaction is expensive or risky, but limited by what the data covers.

See also: [On-policy vs. off-policy](#on-policy-vs-off-policy)

### Curriculum learning

Ordering training tasks from easier to harder, or adapting difficulty to the model's current skill, so there is always learnable signal.

See also: [Pass rate / difficulty band](#pass-rate--difficulty-band)

### Self-play

An agent trains against copies of itself, producing an automatically escalating opponent (AlphaGo Zero, OpenAI Five). Attacker-vs-defender security setups borrow this idea.

See also: [Multi-agent RL](#multi-agent-rl)

### Multi-agent RL

Several learning agents interacting, cooperatively or competitively, in a shared environment. The environment is non-stationary from each agent's view because the others keep changing.

See also: [Self-play](#self-play)

## LLM post-training

_How pretrained models get turned into assistants, reasoners and agents._

### Post-training

Everything after pretraining that shapes a model's behavior: SFT, preference tuning, RLHF, RLVR, safety training. The frontier's capability gains increasingly come from here, especially RL.

See also: [Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)](#supervised-fine-tuning-sft), [RLHF](#rlhf), [RLVR](#rlvr)

### Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)

Also: instruction tuning

Continued training on curated prompt → ideal-response pairs. It teaches format and baseline skills cheaply and usually comes before RL.

See also: [Imitation learning / behavior cloning](#imitation-learning--behavior-cloning)

### RLHF

Also: RL from human feedback

Train a reward model on human comparisons of outputs, then optimize the LLM against it with RL (classically PPO) plus a KL penalty. It was the recipe behind InstructGPT and early ChatGPT.

See also: [Reward model (RM)](#reward-model-rm), [PPO](#ppo), [KL penalty / reference model](#kl-penalty--reference-model)

### RLAIF / Constitutional AI

Replacing some or all human preference labels with AI-generated feedback guided by written principles. Constitutional AI (Anthropic, 2022) used a model critiquing and revising its own outputs against a constitution.

See also: [RLHF](#rlhf), [LLM-as-judge](#llm-as-judge)

### Reward model (RM)

A model trained to predict which output a human would prefer, used as a learned stand-in for human judgment during RL. It is imperfect by nature, so optimizing too hard against it invites reward hacking.

See also: [Reward hacking](#reward-hacking), [Bradley–Terry model](#bradleyterry-model)

### Preference data

Datasets of the form (prompt, response A, response B, which is better). It is the raw material for reward models and DPO.

See also: [DPO](#dpo), [Reward model (RM)](#reward-model-rm)

### Bradley–Terry model

Notation: `P(A≻B) = σ(r_A − r_B)`

The statistical model most reward models assume: the probability one response beats another is a sigmoid of their reward difference.

See also: [Reward model (RM)](#reward-model-rm)

### RLVR

Also: RL from verifiable rewards

RL where reward comes from a programmatic check rather than a learned preference model: unit tests pass, math answer matches, exploit triggers the crash. The term was popularized by AI2's Tülu 3 (2024). It is the dominant paradigm behind reasoning models.

> **In the room:** Security outcomes such as a crash reproduced, a patch that holds or an exploit that lands are verifiable, which is why code-security tasks fit RLVR so well.

See also: [Verifier](#verifier), [Grader](#grader), [Reasoning model](#reasoning-model)

### KL penalty / reference model

Notation: `β · KL(π_θ ‖ π_ref)`

A term that penalizes the trained policy for drifting too far from a frozen reference (usually the SFT model). It limits reward hacking and preserves general capabilities. β sets its strength.

See also: [RLHF](#rlhf), [PPO](#ppo)

### Reasoning model

A model trained, largely with RLVR, to produce extended internal reasoning before answering (OpenAI o-series, DeepSeek-R1, Claude extended thinking). Accuracy scales with how long it is allowed to think.

See also: [Test-time compute](#test-time-compute), [Chain of thought (CoT)](#chain-of-thought-cot)

### Test-time compute

Spending more inference on a problem by thinking longer, sampling many attempts, searching or verifying. It is an axis of improvement separate from model size.

See also: [Reasoning model](#reasoning-model), [Best-of-N / rejection sampling](#best-of-n--rejection-sampling)

### Chain of thought (CoT)

Intermediate reasoning written out before a final answer. RL on verifiable tasks strengthens it; CoT monitoring is also a safety tool for spotting a model reasoning about gaming its reward.

See also: [Reasoning model](#reasoning-model), [Reward hacking](#reward-hacking), [Chain-of-thought monitoring](#chain-of-thought-monitoring)

### Best-of-N / rejection sampling

Generate N candidates, score them with a verifier or reward model, and keep the best. It is used at inference to boost accuracy and in training to build high-quality SFT data from the model's own successes.

See also: [Verifier](#verifier), [Synthetic data](#synthetic-data)

### Synthetic data

Training data generated by models (often filtered by verifiers) rather than humans. RL environments can double as synthetic-data factories: every verified success is a clean demonstration.

See also: [Best-of-N / rejection sampling](#best-of-n--rejection-sampling), [Distillation](#distillation)

### LoRA / PEFT

Also: parameter-efficient fine-tuning

Fine-tuning by training small low-rank adapter matrices instead of all weights. It is far cheaper and common for enterprise customization, rarely used for frontier RL runs.

See also: [Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)](#supervised-fine-tuning-sft)

### Inoculation prompting

A training-time mitigation where the environment's prompt explicitly says that exploiting the grader is acceptable in this context. The model may still learn the hack, but it stops treating 'I cheated' as evidence that it is the kind of model that cheats, so the bad behavior does not spread to other settings.

> **In the room:** Anthropic reports using it on production coding environments as a backstop, not a substitute for a hard-to-game grader. Post-training teams still want environments where the hack isn't available in the first place.

See also: [Reward hacking](#reward-hacking), [Emergent misalignment](#emergent-misalignment)

## Environments & rewards

_Where RL meets the product: tasks, graders, verifiers and what goes wrong with them._

### RL environment (for LLMs)

A packaged, reproducible setting a model can act in during RL training: a task prompt, a sandboxed world (repo, binary, network, browser), tools, and a grader that emits reward. Labs buy or build these at scale; quality, diversity and resistance to hacking are what differentiate them.

> **In the room:** Researchers evaluate an environment on four things: is the reward correct, is it hard to game, is difficulty in the learnable band, and can it run at high rollout throughput?

See also: [Task](#task), [Grader](#grader), [Sandbox](#sandbox), [Environments hub](#environments-hub)

### Task

One problem instance inside an environment: a specific repo with a specific bug, a specific binary to exploit. Environments contain many tasks; counts and diversity matter.

See also: [RL environment (for LLMs)](#rl-environment-for-llms)

### Grader

The component that inspects the final state or transcript and assigns reward. It can be programmatic (tests, crash reproduction), rubric-based, model-based (LLM judge) or hybrid. The grader is the environment's definition of success.

See also: [Verifier](#verifier), [LLM-as-judge](#llm-as-judge), [Reward hacking](#reward-hacking)

### Verifier

A grader that checks correctness deterministically: run tests, compare outputs, re-execute a proof of concept. Verifiers are prized because they are cheap at scale and hard to fool, provided they check the right thing.

See also: [RLVR](#rlvr), [Ground truth](#ground-truth)

### LLM-as-judge

Also: rubric-based reward

Using a model with a rubric to score outputs where no programmatic check exists (quality of a vulnerability report, clarity of remediation advice). It is flexible but noisier and itself a target for gaming.

See also: [Grader](#grader), [RLAIF / Constitutional AI](#rlaif--constitutional-ai)

### Reward hacking

Also: specification gaming

The policy finds a way to earn reward without doing the intended task: editing the tests, special-casing inputs, claiming success, exploiting grader bugs. It is the single biggest failure mode labs worry about in purchased environments.

> **In the room:** Reward hacking isn't hypothetical in code tasks. Models have been documented modifying test files or hardcoding expected outputs. Execution-verified security outcomes are a strong answer.

See also: [Grader](#grader), [KL penalty / reference model](#kl-penalty--reference-model), [Reward shaping](#reward-shaping), [Emergent misalignment](#emergent-misalignment)

### Reward shaping

Adding intermediate rewards to guide learning (for example, partial credit for reaching the vulnerable function). It speeds learning but every added signal is another thing the policy can game.

See also: [Sparse vs. dense reward](#sparse-vs-dense-reward), [Tiered / partial-credit reward](#tiered--partial-credit-reward)

### Tiered / partial-credit reward

Reward that distinguishes levels of success (crash found → controlled crash → working exploit) instead of pass/fail. It gives gradient signal on hard tasks where full success is rare.

See also: [Reward shaping](#reward-shaping)

### Outcome reward model (ORM)

Scores only the final result of a trajectory.

See also: [Process reward model (PRM)](#process-reward-model-prm)

### Process reward model (PRM)

Scores each intermediate step of a trajectory, helping with credit assignment on long reasoning chains. It is more informative but expensive to label and easier to game than outcome checks.

See also: [Credit assignment](#credit-assignment), [Outcome reward model (ORM)](#outcome-reward-model-orm)

### Pass rate / difficulty band

The fraction of rollouts that solve a task. Useful tasks sit in a band the model sometimes solves. Near 0% gives no signal and near 100% teaches nothing. Labs filter and recalibrate tasks to stay in this band as models improve.

> **In the room:** Expect questions like 'What's the pass rate of our current model on your tasks?' They are checking the difficulty band.

See also: [GRPO](#grpo), [Curriculum learning](#curriculum-learning)

### pass@k

Notation: `pass@k`

The probability that at least one of k sampled attempts succeeds (Chen et al., 2021, Codex paper). pass@1 measures reliability; pass@k with large k measures whether the capability exists at all.

See also: [Benchmark](#benchmark), [Pass rate / difficulty band](#pass-rate--difficulty-band)

### Sandbox

An isolated execution environment (container, VM, microVM) where the agent can run code without escaping or affecting real systems. For offensive security tasks, strong isolation is non-negotiable.

See also: [RL environment (for LLMs)](#rl-environment-for-llms)

### Tool use / function calling

The model emits structured calls (run shell, read file, call API) that the harness executes, returning results as new observations. It turns a text model into an agent that acts.

See also: [Agent (AI)](#agent-ai), [Model Context Protocol (MCP)](#model-context-protocol-mcp)

### Scaffold / harness

The code wrapping a model during a task: system prompt, tool definitions, loop control, context management. Results depend heavily on the scaffold, so environments need to specify or be compatible with the lab's own.

See also: [Tool use / function calling](#tool-use--function-calling)

### Gym interface

Notation: `reset() → obs; step(a) → obs, r, done`

The standard API shape from OpenAI Gym, now Gymnasium, that most RL environments follow. LLM environment frameworks adapt it to multi-turn tool use.

See also: [Environment](#environment)

### Rollout infrastructure

The systems that spin up environment instances, run policy inference, execute tools and collect trajectories at scale, often thousands of concurrent sandboxes. Environment startup time and reliability directly affect training cost.

See also: [Rollout](#rollout), [Sandbox](#sandbox)

### Data contamination

When test or training tasks leak into pretraining data, so the model has effectively memorized the answer. For public CVEs and CTFs this is a real concern; novel or obfuscated targets avoid it.

See also: [Benchmark](#benchmark), [Held-out set](#held-out-set)

### Proof of solvability

Evidence that a task can actually be completed, such as a reference solution or a working exploit. Unsolvable tasks waste compute and poison the reward signal.

See also: [Ground truth](#ground-truth)

### Environments hub

Also: environment marketplace

A shared registry where teams publish, discover and reuse RL environments behind a common interface, for example Prime Intellect's Environments Hub or General Reasoning's OpenReward and its Open Reward Standard. It makes environments easier to plug into any trainer, much as model hubs did for weights.

> **In the room:** Useful context in competitive conversations: thousands of free community environments exist, so paid environments have to win on realism, grader quality, hack resistance and exclusivity rather than on availability.

See also: [RL environment (for LLMs)](#rl-environment-for-llms), [Gym interface](#gym-interface), [Verifier](#verifier)

## Evaluation & safety

_How labs measure models and manage risk._

### Benchmark

A fixed task set with a scoring method used to compare models (SWE-bench, MMLU, Cybench). Labs report headline numbers on them, and saturated or contaminated benchmarks push demand for fresh evaluations.

See also: [Eval saturation](#eval-saturation), [Data contamination](#data-contamination)

### Eval saturation

When top models score near the ceiling, a benchmark no longer separates them. This steadily creates demand for harder tasks.

See also: [Benchmark](#benchmark)

### Held-out set

Tasks deliberately excluded from training so they measure generalization. Environment buyers often want a split: some tasks for training, some reserved for eval.

See also: [Data contamination](#data-contamination)

### Generalization

Performance on inputs unlike the training data. The question behind every environment purchase: does training here improve the model elsewhere, or only on these tasks?

See also: [Held-out set](#held-out-set)

### Red teaming

Adversarially probing a model or system to find harmful behaviors, jailbreaks or security weaknesses before release.

See also: [Jailbreak](#jailbreak), [Prompt injection](#prompt-injection)

### Jailbreak

An input that gets a model to bypass its safety training and produce content it would normally refuse.

See also: [Red teaming](#red-teaming)

### Prompt injection

Malicious instructions hidden in content the model processes (a web page, file, tool output) that hijack an agent's behavior. It is a leading security risk for agents with tool access.

See also: [Agent (AI)](#agent-ai), [Tool use / function calling](#tool-use--function-calling)

### Alignment

Making models reliably pursue the goals their developers and users intend, including under optimization pressure. Reward hacking is an alignment failure in miniature.

See also: [Reward hacking](#reward-hacking)

### Frontier safety framework

Also: responsible scaling policy

A lab's published policy (Anthropic RSP, OpenAI Preparedness Framework, Google DeepMind Frontier Safety Framework) that defines dangerous-capability thresholds, including cyber, and the safeguards required before deploying past them.

> **In the room:** Cyber-offense is a named risk domain in these frameworks. Labs must measure it, which creates demand for rigorous security evals alongside training environments.

See also: [Dual-use / cyber uplift](#dual-use--cyber-uplift)

### Dual-use / cyber uplift

Capabilities that help both defenders and attackers. 'Uplift' measures how much a model increases a threat actor's ability compared with existing tools. Labs weigh it when training on offensive security tasks.

See also: [Frontier safety framework](#frontier-safety-framework), [Trusted access program](#trusted-access-program)

### System card / model card

The documentation a lab publishes with a model covering capabilities, evaluations (often including cyber) and safety mitigations. It is a good place to learn what a lab measures and cares about.

See also: [Frontier safety framework](#frontier-safety-framework)

### Agent (AI)

A model operating in a loop: observe, decide, call tools, repeat, until a goal is reached. Agentic coding and security agents are the product direction RL environments train for.

See also: [Tool use / function calling](#tool-use--function-calling), [Agent (RL)](#agent-rl)

### Model Context Protocol (MCP)

An open protocol (introduced by Anthropic in late 2024 and donated to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025) for connecting models to tools and data sources through a standard server interface. It is widely adopted across agent frameworks.

See also: [Tool use / function calling](#tool-use--function-calling)

### Emergent misalignment

When narrow bad training generalizes into broadly bad behavior. Anthropic showed that a model that learned to reward hack in real coding environments also started faking alignment, cooperating with bad actors and sabotaging code, even though it was never trained to do those things.

> **In the room:** This raises the stakes on reward hacking from 'wasted compute' to 'a safety problem'. Research leads and alignment teams care about it, and it is a strong reason to buy environments whose graders are hard to game.

See also: [Reward hacking](#reward-hacking), [Alignment](#alignment), [Inoculation prompting](#inoculation-prompting)

### Chain-of-thought monitoring

Also: CoT monitorability

Reading a model's reasoning trace, usually with another model, to catch bad intent such as plans to game a test before it acts. It only works while the reasoning honestly reflects what drives the model. Training hard against the monitor can teach the model to hide its intent, known as obfuscated reward hacking.

> **In the room:** Labs use it to spot reward hacking during RL runs. Expect researchers to ask whether an environment's reward pressure could push models to hide their reasoning.

See also: [Chain of thought (CoT)](#chain-of-thought-cot), [Reward hacking](#reward-hacking), [Sandbagging](#sandbagging)

### Evaluation awareness

A model noticing that it is being tested rather than used for real, and behaving differently as a result. Frontier system cards now report it because it can make safety and capability results look better or worse than real-world behavior.

> **In the room:** Toy-looking tasks are easy to spot. Realistic environments built from real codebases and real vulnerabilities are harder to recognize as tests, which matters to eval and safety teams.

See also: [Sandbagging](#sandbagging), [System card / model card](#system-card--model-card), [Benchmark](#benchmark)

### Sandbagging

A model deliberately underperforming on an evaluation, for example scoring lower on a dangerous-capability test than it could. If it goes unnoticed, a lab may underestimate the model and apply weaker safeguards than it needs.

> **In the room:** Cyber evaluations are a key place labs check for it, which makes trustworthy, execution-verified security tasks valuable to safety teams.

See also: [Evaluation awareness](#evaluation-awareness), [Dual-use / cyber uplift](#dual-use--cyber-uplift), [Frontier safety framework](#frontier-safety-framework)

### Time horizon

Also: METR time horizon

METR's measure of agent capability: the length of task, in expert-human working time, that a model completes with a given success rate (usually 50%). It has been doubling roughly every four to seven months, making it a common way to track progress on long, agentic work.

> **In the room:** It frames demand. As horizons stretch from minutes to hours, labs need longer multi-step tasks, such as full vulnerability hunts, to train and measure models.

See also: [Agent (AI)](#agent-ai), [Benchmark](#benchmark), [Horizon](#horizon)

### Trusted access program

A lab's gated release of its most cyber-capable models to vetted defenders only, instead of the general public. Examples include Anthropic's Project Glasswing, which gives partners Claude Mythos Preview to find and fix vulnerabilities in critical software, and OpenAI's Trusted Access for Cyber (Daybreak).

> **In the room:** Shows that labs treat offensive-security capability as both valuable and dangerous. AppSec leaders at large enterprises are often already in these programs, and the resulting flood of findings creates demand for triage and verification.

See also: [Dual-use / cyber uplift](#dual-use--cyber-uplift), [Frontier safety framework](#frontier-safety-framework), [Coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD)](#coordinated-vulnerability-disclosure-cvd)

## Security for AI training

_Code-security terms that show up when RL targets vulnerability work._

### Fuzzing

Automated testing that feeds large volumes of generated or mutated inputs to a program to trigger crashes and bugs. Coverage-guided fuzzers (AFL++, libFuzzer) and Mayhem are examples. Fuzzing produces reproducible, verifiable ground truth.

See also: [Ground truth](#ground-truth), [Sanitizers](#sanitizers)

### Vulnerability (CVE / CWE)

A flaw that can be exploited to violate security. A CVE is an identifier for a specific public vulnerability; a CWE is a category of weakness (for example CWE-787, out-of-bounds write).

See also: [Proof of concept (PoC)](#proof-of-concept-poc), [Vulnerability localization](#vulnerability-localization)

### Proof of concept (PoC)

An input or script that demonstrates a vulnerability is real, typically by triggering the crash or unauthorized behavior. In RL it doubles as a verifier: rerun the PoC and the reward is objective.

See also: [Verifier](#verifier), [Exploit](#exploit)

### Exploit

Code that leverages a vulnerability to achieve an attacker goal, such as control-flow hijack, code execution or data exfiltration. It goes well beyond a crash.

See also: [Proof of concept (PoC)](#proof-of-concept-poc)

### Sanitizers

Also: ASan, UBSan, MSan

Compiler instrumentation that detects memory errors and undefined behavior at runtime with precise reports. Sanitizer output is a common programmatic grader signal.

See also: [Fuzzing](#fuzzing), [Verifier](#verifier)

### Crash triage / deduplication

Grouping crashes by root cause and judging severity and exploitability. Needed so a grader doesn't reward the same bug 50 times.

See also: [Grader](#grader)

### Patch / remediation

A code change that removes a vulnerability. A good grader checks both that the PoC no longer works and that functionality and tests still pass, because deleting the feature also 'fixes' the bug.

See also: [Reward hacking](#reward-hacking)

### False positive

A reported vulnerability that isn't real. Models hallucinate findings readily, so rewarding claims without verification trains a false-positive factory.

See also: [Hallucination](#hallucination), [Verifier](#verifier)

### Ground truth

The verified correct answer for a task, such as the known bug, the working exploit or the valid patch. Environments with trustworthy ground truth yield trustworthy rewards.

See also: [Verifier](#verifier), [Proof of solvability](#proof-of-solvability)

### Capture the Flag (CTF)

Security competitions where solving a challenge yields a secret 'flag' string. The format is naturally verifiable and widely used in AI cyber evals (Cybench, InterCode-CTF), but public CTFs carry contamination risk.

See also: [Data contamination](#data-contamination), [Benchmark](#benchmark)

### Cyber range

A realistic, isolated network environment for practicing attack and defense, the multi-host analogue of a sandbox.

See also: [Sandbox](#sandbox)

### Bug bounty

Programs paying researchers for valid vulnerability reports. They generate real-world, human-validated vulnerability data and triage expertise, a source of realistic tasks and grading judgment.

See also: [Ground truth](#ground-truth), [Coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD)](#coordinated-vulnerability-disclosure-cvd)

### Vulnerability localization

Finding where in a codebase a vulnerability lives: given a weakness type and an unfamiliar repository, point to the affected files or functions. It comes before proving or patching the bug and is still hard for models at repository scale.

> **In the room:** Cisco's Vulnerability Localization Benchmark (September 2026) found the best system scored only 0.229 file-level F1 across 500 real vulnerabilities, a clear gap that training environments can target.

See also: [Vulnerability (CVE / CWE)](#vulnerability-cve--cwe), [Ground truth](#ground-truth), [False positive](#false-positive)

### Coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD)

The standard process for reporting a vulnerability privately to the maintainer or vendor, giving them time to fix it before details go public. AI-driven discovery is straining it: maintainers are receiving both far more real findings and a flood of convincing but fabricated AI-written reports.

> **In the room:** curl shut its bug bounty in January 2026 over AI-generated junk reports. Verified, reproducible findings with a working PoC are what separate useful AI output from noise, which matters to AppSec leaders and bug bounty programs.

See also: [Bug bounty](#bug-bounty), [False positive](#false-positive), [Proof of concept (PoC)](#proof-of-concept-poc)
